input.prompt:
You are given one document: `corpora/docs_b/SDX7_PROTOCOL_SPEC_v3.1.md` (path relative to the
task-set root). It is a synthetic protocol specification whose normative requirements are
spread over sections 2 to 9, with an errata list in section 10.

TASK

List every requirement that is at level `MUST` in the specification **as corrected by the
errata**, across all normative sections.

Section 1 states how the errata interact with the body: an errata entry that gives a corrected
level supersedes the level printed in the body; an entry marked **Withdrawn** removes the
requirement from the normative set entirely, whatever level the body printed; and an entry
marked **Clarified** is editorial and leaves the body's level standing.

Note that `MUST` and `MUST NOT` are different levels. Only `MUST` is in scope.

Each record has exactly these keys:

  req_id            string, e.g. "SDX-REQ-0042"
  section           integer, the number of the `## n.` section the requirement is printed in
  constrained_field string, the field name the requirement names, without backticks
  level_source      string, "errata" if this requirement's level comes from an errata entry
                    that gave a corrected level, otherwise "body"

Normalisation rules (they define exact match; do not substitute your own):

N1. A date is written as `YYYY-MM-DD`. A UTC instant is written as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`.
N2. A quantity is a JSON number with no units, no currency symbol, no thousands separator and
    no trailing zeroes beyond what the document prints (write 4.5, not 4.50; write 30, not 30.0).
N3. A yes/no value is a JSON boolean.
N4. A text value is copied verbatim from the document, without markdown emphasis characters,
    without surrounding quotation marks, and without the numerals a clause may print in
    brackets after a spelled-out number.
N5. Where a value is spelled out in words and repeated as a numeral in brackets - for example
    "ninety (90) days" - the numeral is the value.
N6. Reply with a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose before or after it, no markdown
    code fence.

Output exactly this object:

{
  "requirements": [ { ...record... }, ... ],
  "count": <integer, equal to the length of requirements>
}

`requirements` must be sorted by `req_id` ascending.

expected_behavior: The run collects every requirement and its printed level, applies the errata by kind - relevel, withdraw, clarify - distinguishes MUST from MUST NOT, and emits the sorted record set. Requirements promoted to MUST by the errata are present; requirements demoted away from MUST or withdrawn are absent; `level_source` is `errata` only where a corrected level was given.
quality_metric: Records are matched on `req_id`, with 4 comparable cells per key record. A cell matches when the reported record exists and the value equals the key's after normalisation. Every cell of a key record with no reported counterpart counts as 4 mismatches. Every reported record whose `req_id` is not in the key adds 4 to the denominator and contributes 0 matches. quality_score = matched_cells / denominator, rounded to 4 decimal places. `count` disagreeing with the length of `requirements` subtracts 0.05 (floor 0). task_success = true iff quality_score >= 0.97.
failure_condition: Outright failure if any of: (1) the reply is not parseable as a single JSON object with the two required keys; (2) quality_score < 0.97 (frozen workload-B floor); (3) any record reports a `req_id` that does not appear in the document - a fabricated requirement; (4) the run edits the source document.
notes: Ignoring the errata entirely still yields a plausible answer of the same size, but with several wrong members; the MUST / MUST NOT distinction is a second, independent trap.
